docs.title: Ghost stabilisation
docs.text:
The non-mesh-matching nature of the Material Point Method (MPM) means that small overlaps between material point domains and background mesh elements can generate vanishingly small mass and stiffness contributions at certain nodes . These small-cut interactions degrade the conditioning of the resulting global linear system of equations and often produce spurious stress oscillations near the physical boundary of the body.

For implicit MPM formulations using generalised interpolation basis functions, two stabilisation strategies currently exist: ghost stabilisation and mesh aggregation. This code adopts ghost stabilisation, which introduces a penalty term into the mass and/or stiffness matrix to control the gradient of the solution across background mesh faces adjacent to the boundary of the physical body. This restores coercivity, improves the conditioning of the linear system, and significantly enhances solution quality in boundary regions.

docs.title: Small cut instability
docs.text:
Without stabilisation the material point method has the potential to be highly unstable. This is because the nature of the linear system of equations being solved is highly dependent on the positioning of material points relative to the background grid. There is the potential for very small values of mass/stiffness to be generated at background grid degrees of freedom if small overlaps are generated between the physical body (i.e. the material points) and the background grid. This can result in large spurious incremental displacements/velocities/accelerations being generated at the boundary of the physical body, which have the potential to lead to failure of the numerical solver within a time step. An example of this is shown below for a quasi-static elasto-plastic collapse problem, where at a given time step the original, non-stabilised, Generalised Interpolation Material Point Method (GIMPM) predicts very large spurious incremental nodal displacements, which are removed with stabilisation.

Figure 1: Elasto-plastic collapse: background mesh incremental displacements

To explore this issue in more detail, consider the simpler problem shown in Figure 2, where a block of material is displaced with a value of \(a\), as a rigid body through a 2D background mesh with element size \(h\). The condition number (the ratio of the largest to smallest eigenvalue) of the mass and stiffness matrices are determined at each displaced solution. The test case assumes linear elastic material behaviour with a Young's modulus of \(E=1\) Pa, a Poisson's ratio of \(\nu=0\) and a density of \(\rho=1~\text{kg/m}^3\).

Figure 2: Rigid translation test case and the resulting unstabilised condition numbers. Use the arrows to displace the body by a through the background mesh of element size h; the purple line marks the current a/h on the GIMPM panel.

Figure 2 also provides the condition numbers, \(\kappa([\cdot])\), of the unstabilised consistent mass, \([M_v]\), lumped mass, \([\bar{M}_v]\), and stiffness, \([K]\), matrices for the standard Material Point Method (MPM) and the GIMPM. Although the stiffness matrix for the standard MPM is well behaved, all other matrices show condition number spikes generate by small material point-background mesh node interactions. Large condition numbers cause problems when solving linear systems of equations when the precision of the calculations are no longer capable of resolving the span of entries in the system, leading to loss of accuracy and in the case, boundary artifacts and stability issues. The grey shaded region on the MPM plot highlights where the physical material is no longer constrained in the horizontal direction by the pinned boundary condition. It is appropriate that \(\kappa([K])=\infty\) in this case.

docs.title: Boundary identification
docs.text:
A central requirement of ghost stabilisation is determining which element faces lie on or near the physical boundary of the body. Unlike unfitted finite element methods, most Material Point Method simulations do not explicitly track the geometry of the physical domain. As a result, we need a robust way to identify these boundary faces without reconstructing or tracking the boundary itself.

The process consists of two steps (shown graphically in Figure 4):

  • Boundary element detection: first boundary elements are identified as the elements that share a face with any unpopulated element.
  • Boundary face extraction: relevant faces are then defined as those belonging to boundary elements that border either: another boundary element; or an element populated by material points.

These faces are stabilised. Each of the faces will connect two elements, one of which is labelled as the positive element, \(K^+\), and the other the negative element, \(K^-\). The labelling is arbitrary and flipping positive/negative elements has no impact of the stabilisation.

Figure 2: MPM boundary element identification

The stabilisation of the faces between between boundary elements and active (populated) elements is important as it enforces gradient continuity between the well-conditioned interior region and the partially filled boundary elements, greatly improving stability. For simulations involving multiple bodies defined by material point, the procedure is applied independently to each body, and the stabilisation faces are taken as the union of all identified faces.

docs.title: Ghost stabilsation
docs.text:
The ghost stabilisation term for linear elements can be expressed as

\[ j(u_i,w_i) = \frac{h^{3}}{3} \int_{\Gamma} \left( \frac{\partial u^+_i}{\partial x_j}n_j- \frac{\partial u^-_i}{\partial x_j}n_j\right) \left( \frac{\partial w^+_i}{\partial x_j}n_j- \frac{\partial w^-_i}{\partial x_j}n_j\right) d\Gamma, \]

where \(h\) is the background mesh grid size, \(u_i\) and \(w_i\) are the test and trial functions, \(x_j\) are the Cartesian coordinates, \(n_j\) is the outward normal to the face of the positive element (see Figure 5) and \(\Gamma\) are the boundary element faces that require stabilisation.

Figure 3: Boundary stabilisation normal and positive/negative elements

Introducing the finite element approximation space for the test and trial functions and eliminating the nodal values associated with the test function (full derivation given in Coombs (2023)) results in a matrix comprised of four sub components multiplied by the physical displacements of the positive, \(\{d^+\}\), and negative, \(\{d^-\}\), elements

\[ \{f_G\} = \left[\begin{array}{cc} {[J_G^{++}]} & [J_G^{+-}] \\ {[J_G^{-+}]} & [J_G^{--}] \end{array} \right]\left\{\begin{array}{c} \{d^+\}\\ \{d^-\} \end{array}\right\} = [J_G]\{d\}, \]

the combined \([J_G]\) matrix can be compactly expressed as

\[ [J_G] = \frac{h^{3}}{3} \int_{\Gamma} \Bigl([G]^T[m][G]\Bigr) d\Gamma, \qquad \text{where} \qquad [G] = \Bigl[ [G^+] \quad -[G^-] \Bigr] \]

and \([m]=[n][n]^T\).

For three dimensional analysis are the normal matrix associated with the positive element, \([n]\), and the matrix containing the shape function derivatives, \([G^+]\), are

\[ [n]^T = \left[\begin{array}{cccccc} n_x & 0 & 0 & n_y & 0 & n_z\\ 0 & n_y & 0 & n_x & n_z & 0\\ 0 & 0 & n_z & 0 & n_y & n_x \end{array}\right] \]

and

\[ [G^+] = \left[\begin{array}{ccc c ccc} {N_1^+}_{,x} & 0 & 0 & \ldots & {N_n^+}_{,x} & 0 & 0\\ 0 & {N_1^+}_{,y} & 0 & \ldots & 0 & {N_n^+}_{,y} & 0\\ 0 & 0 & {N_1^+}_{,z} & \ldots & 0 & 0 & {N_n^+}_{,z}\\ {N_1^+}_{,y} & {N_1^+}_{,x} & 0 & \ldots & {N_n^+}_{,y} & {N_n^+}_{,x} & 0\\ 0 & {N_1^+}_{,z} & {N_1^+}_{,y} & \ldots & 0 & {N_n^+}_{,z} & {N_n^+}_{,y}\\ {N_1^+}_{,z} & 0 & {N_1^+}_{,x} & \ldots & {N_n^+}_{,z} & 0 & {N_n^+}_{,x}\\ \end{array}\right]. \]

where \(N_i\) are the basis functions of the background finite element mesh and \(n\) is the number of nodes associated with the positive element.

docs.title: Stiffness stabilisation
docs.text:
For quasi-static analysis, ghost stabilisation acts as a penalty approach that modifies the weak form of the equilibrium equation to

\[ \int_{\varphi_t(K)}[\nabla_x S_{vp}]^{T}\{\sigma_p\} \text{d}V - \int_{\varphi_t(K)}[S_{vp}]^{T}\{b\} \text{d}V + \beta_k \int_{\Gamma} [G]^T[n]\{g\} d\Gamma= \{0\}, \]

where \(\{g\}=[n]^T[G]\{d\}\) is the jump in the displacement over a boundary element edge, \(\beta_k = \gamma_k h^3/3\) and \(\gamma_k\) is a ghost stabilisation stiffness penalty parameter that controls the magnitude of the ghost stabilisation.

Linearising the ghost stabilisation term in the weak equilibrium equation with respect to the unknown displacements of the background mesh results in a stiffness stabilisation term with the following form

\[ {[K_G]} = \frac{\gamma_k h^3}{3} \int_{\Gamma} \Bigl([G]^T[m][G]\Bigr) d\Gamma = \gamma_k {[J_G]} \]

docs.title: Mass stabilisation
docs.text:
For dynamic problems, the consistent mass matrix can be stabilised by the addition of

\[ [M_G] = \gamma_M [J_G] \]

where \(\gamma_M\) is the ghost stabilisation mass penalty parameter, which is typically to set \(\gamma_M=\rho/4\), where \(\rho\) is the density of the material being analysed.

Note that the sum of the rows/columns in \([J_G]\) is equal to zero. This means that no additional physical mass is introduced into the linear system. However, it also means that stabilising the consistent mass matrix and then lumping entries into a diagonal lumped mass matrix removes any stabilisation in the resultant matrix.

docs.title: Practical application
docs.text: The implemented MPM software includes stiffness matrix ghost stabilisation as standard for all quasi-static and dynamic analyses. It is possible to apply stiffness and mass stabilisation when using implicit methods to solve dynamic problems, however it has been found that stiffness stabilisation is sufficient to mitigate the small cut instability.

docs.title: Penalty parameter value
docs.text:
The stiffness penalty parameter is set to

\[ \gamma_k = \frac{\bar{E}}{30} \]

where \(\bar{E}\) is the volume weighted average Young's modulus of the material points that occupy the elements that share the element boundary where the stabilisation is applied.

docs.title: Numerical integration
docs.text:
The integrals required to calculate \([K_G]\) are evaluated using standard Gauss-Legendre quadrature on each stabilised face

\[ {[K_G]} = \frac{\gamma_k h^3}{3} \sum_{i=1}^{n_{Gp}}\Bigl([G_i]^T[m][G_i]\det([J])w_i\Bigr) \]

where \(n_{Gp}\) is the number of Gauss points, \(w_i\) is the weight associated with the Gauss point and \([J]\) is the Jacobian that links the local face and global coordinate systems. The determinant of \([J]\) provides the ratio of the global to local areas of the face; for cubic elements \(\det([J])=h^2/4\). Note that \([G]\) can vary between Gauss points whereas \([m]\) is constant for a given face. The polynomial order of the terms in \([K_G]\) means that a 2-by-2 grid of quadrature points is used, such that \(n_{Gp}=4\). The local positions of the Gauss points are tied to the positive element. The local positions on the negative element determined through a robust local-to-global-to-local coordinate map that avoids the implementation of case by case algorithms.

On octree meshes, the integration is performed over the face of the smallest element when applying stabilisation on non-matching faces. This choice avoids over penalising the smaller background mesh elements.

docs.title: Tutorial problems
docs.text:
The MPM3S tutorial set walks you through benchmark problems, each one isolating a different capability of the solver - large deformation under self-weight, rigid-body contact, plastic soil, dynamic time integration, articulated rigid bodies, and adaptive mesh refinement following a moving body. Every tutorial uses the same input_data.json format, so once you've completed Tutorial 1 the workflow is the same the whole way through; later tutorials add capabilities one at a time.

The recommended order is top to bottom - each tutorial reuses material settings, contact settings or solver choices established in earlier ones.

Before starting, install Julia and MPM3S as described in MPM3S installation.

docs.title: Static
docs.text:
Quasi-static problems solved with Newton-Raphson over a sequence of load steps.

  • Tutorial 1 - Self-weight column - An elastic column compressed by its own weight. The simplest problem in the set: no contact, no plasticity and no mesh refinement, but large deformation, with an analytical vertical stress solution to validate the numerical result against. Introduces the input file, running MPM3S and viewing the output with the option to extend the analysis for convergence tests.
  • Tutorial 2 - Compaction via a rigid body - A cube compressed by a rigid cude through 25% of its height. Introduces rigid bodies defined by an STL surface, prescribed displacements and penalty contact.
  • Tutorial 3 - Vertical penetration (CPT) - A quarter-symmetric cone penetration test in dry sand. Adds a two-stage analysis, Willam-Warnke sand with depth-dependent stiffness, frictional contact and mesh refinement that follows the cone.
  • Tutorial 4 - Plough (horizontal penetration) (coming soon) - A seabed cable plough dragged through dry sand. The most geometrically complex problem: a non-convex rigid body, a Signorini exit-face condition, and adaptive refinement that travels with the plough across 20 m of horizontal travel.

docs.title: Dynamic
docs.text:
Implicit dynamic problems using the same Newton-Raphson framework but with inertia and time integration active.

  • Tutorial 5 - Rolling sphere - A rigid sphere rolling down a 45° slope, with a friction-coefficient sweep validated against the analytical slip/stick solution. Introduces dynamic stages, a free rigid body and a boundary track that follows the sphere.
  • Tutorial 6 - Drag anchor - A half-symmetric AC-14 drag anchor pulled through very loose, submerged sand. Combines Tutorial 3's soil model and Tutorial 5's dynamics and moving boundaries with an anchor made of two hinged parts, an angle stop and a pull line, over three analysis stages.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
This quick start tutorial walks through the steps of running your first MPM3S problem.

This tutorial analyses a column deforming under its own weight and solves the static equilibrium equations. It is simple but introduces you to all components of the code: setting up the input file, running the analysis and viewing the output data.

This tutorial has three main sections after the introduction:

  • Input setup
  • Deploying and running the problem
  • Viewing the results

docs.title: Background: the GIMPM
docs.text:
This problem introduces you to the MPM3S code, and how it is different to methods such as finite element analysis. The GIMPM can be classed as a fictitious domain method: the mesh and boundary conditions do not necessarily align with the material domain, the body that is being modelled by the material points. This enables the GIMPM to avoid the distorted mesh issues normally associated with finite elements.

The GIMPM broadly works in three steps: Figure 1: The three steps to a GIMPM solution step.

  • (a) initial state which loads the material point data on the background mesh
  • (b) deforming the mesh and the material points together
  • (c) resetting the mesh but not the material points, distorting the body relative to the mesh

Under this framework you define two things: the background mesh on which the equations are solved, through its element size, and the material points - the modelled body, which carries all the material and kinematic data at the Generalised Interpolation Material Points (GIMPs). In MPM3S both are set in the "material points" section of the input file. Boundary conditions (roller or fixed faces) are applied to the nodes of the background mesh, whereas body forces such as gravity are applied to the material points directly.

docs.title: Problem summary
docs.text:
The aim is to recover the vertical stress field that develops in a column compressed by its own weight, and to compare it against the analytical solution

\[ \sigma_{zz} = -\rho\, g\, (L - z_p), \]

where \(\rho\) is the density, \(g = 9.81\) m/s\(^2\) is the acceleration due to gravity, \(L = 0.8\) m is the initial height of the column and \(z_p\) is the initial height of the material point. Stress is tension positive, so the column is in compression. Because Poisson's ratio is zero and the sides of the column are on rollers, the cross-section does not change and this Cauchy stress calculation is true for any magnitude of deformation.

The column is \(0.05 \times 0.05 \times 0.8\) m, made of a homogeneous Hencky elastic material with Poisson's ratio \(\nu = 0\) and density \(\rho = 50\) kg/m\(^3\). The Young's modulus, \(E = 283\) Pa, is chosen so the column will be significantly compressed from \(0.8\) m to about \(0.54\) m.

The column is divided into 16 elements of \(0.05\) m, each filled with a \(2 \times 2 \times 2\) grid of GIMPs - 128 in total. Gravity is applied gradually over 50 load steps, each solved by a Newton-Raphson scheme.

Figure 2: The bottom two elements and the top element of the column; the dots stand for the 13 elements in between. (a) The background mesh, with element size \(h = 0.05\) m, and (b) the \(2 \times 2 \times 2\) grid of GIMP domains in each element.

The simulation is configured through a single JSON object - a human-readable, editable text file. The complete file for this problem can be found here, and every key is described on the input_data.json file format page.

docs.title: Machine
docs.text:
"GPU": "off" runs the analysis on the CPU, which is plenty for a problem this small.

"domain update": "stretch" lets the domain of each GIMP stretch with the deformation of the material, so that the GIMPs near the base shrink to half their height as the column is compressed. It is optional; without it the domains keep their initial size.

docs.title: Domain
docs.text: The background mesh is a cube sized automatically to hold the column plus the same height of empty space above it, which here makes it a cube of side \(1.6\) m. Gravity acts in \(-z\).

docs.title: Material points
docs.text:
The column is one layer, \(0.8\) m thick, on a \(0.05 \times 0.05\) m footprint. "element size" sets the background elements to \(0.05\) m, and "number of material points per element 1": 2 places a \(2 \times 2 \times 2\) grid of GIMPs in each element.

The material is the Hencky elastic model with the parameters from the Problem summary. "extra capacity" reserves spare storage for material points created by mesh refinement; there is no refinement here, but the key is still required.

docs.title: Rigid bodies and contact
docs.text: This problem has no rigid bodies, so "rigid bodies" is an empty list. The "contact" section is still required, and its friction coefficient has no effect.

docs.title: Analysis
docs.text:
A single static stage. "load": "gravity ramp" increases gravity from zero to its full value over the 50 load steps, and "rigid bodies": "off" because there are none.

Rollers are applied on the four sides (\(x\) and \(y\) "min" and "max") and the base is fixed. The top is left free; the "max" \(z\) face lies at twice the column height, in the empty space above the column, so it never touches the material.

docs.title: Solver
docs.text: Each load step is solved by Newton-Raphson iterations to a tolerance of \(10^{-6}\); a step that has not converged after 20 iterations is retried with half the load increment. The column fills its elements completely, so the ghost stabilisation is switched off with both ghost factors set to zero.

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
VTK output, for visualisation in ParaView (or VisIt), is written to vtk_column at every load step ("vtk percent": 0), with the displacement, stress, strain and volume of each GIMP.

CSV output is written to csv_column, also at every load step, with each GIMP's initial position, current position and stress - everything needed to compare against the analytical solution. There are no rigid bodies, so no rigid-body fields are needed.

docs.text:
The input file for this tutorial comes with MPM3S, as validation_data_and_jsons/input_data_gravity_column.json; it is the same file as the one provided here.

Open a terminal and start Julia; -t auto makes every CPU core available:

julia -t auto

Then, in Julia, move into the folder where you downloaded MPM3S, activate it and load MPM3S:

cd("path/to/MPM3S")
using Pkg; Pkg.activate(".")
using MPM3S

The output folders vtk_column and csv_column are created in the MPM3S folder. The commands work the same on Windows, macOS and Linux. If you are unsure how to open a command/terminal window on your operating system, see Command/terminal window.

docs.title: Running the problem
docs.text:
Julia is now running in the MPM3S folder and MPM3S loaded. The JSON file for this problem is loaded with MPM3S and is stored in the folder validation_data_and_jsons, the simulations are started with:

MPM3S.non_linear_solve("validation_data_and_jsons/input_data_gravity_column.json");
This reads the input file, steps through the 50 load steps and writes the VTK and CSV output as it goes.

docs.title: Reading the output
docs.text:
MPM3S prints a single progress line, redrawn in place after every step; in a log file a new line is kept for every whole percent. When the analysis finishes, the line reads:

  • stage 1/1 - the current stage and the number of stages.
  • the bar and 100.0% - progress through the stage.
  • t 1.0/1.0 - the load fraction reached in a static stage (or the time in a dynamic stage), out of its final value.
  • step 51 - the step counter. It starts at 1 and counts every converged step of the analysis; it is also the number in the output file names.
  • Δt 0.02 - the current increment, here \(1/50\) of the load.
  • NR 3 - the Newton-Raphson iterations used by the last step.
  • cuts 0 - steps that did not converge and were retried with half the increment.
  • del 0 - material points deleted because they became too distorted or isolated.
  • N 257 - the number of nodes in the background mesh.

In dynamic analyses a P2G-fail count is added if a velocity projection fails to converge.

docs.title: Viewing the results
docs.text: The results are written as the simulation runs, so you do not need to wait until it has finished to view them. The VTK files are in vtk_column and the CSV files in csv_column, one file per load step, numbered from 00002 to 00051. The 1 in mps_1_... is the layer number.

3. Apply the reader. Click Apply in the Properties panel. The column of GIMPs appears at the first load step.

Figure 5: The series in the Pipeline Browser, with Apply highlighted in the Properties panel.

  • Middle-click and drag (or Shift+left-drag) to pan.
  • Scroll wheel (or right-click and drag) to zoom in and out.
  • Press R or use View → Reset Camera to reframe the scene if you get lost.

4. Colour the GIMPs by vertical displacement. Change Coloring to displacement → Z. At the first load step the displacements are still small.

Figure 6: The column of GIMPs at the first load step, with displacement chosen in the Coloring menu.

5. Advance to the final step. Click the Go to Last button (▶|) in the time toolbar, then Rescale to Data Range in the colour-bar toolbar so the colour scale matches the deformed column. The column has shortened from \(0.8\) m to about \(0.54\) m, so the top has moved down by about \(0.26\) m.

Figure 7: The deformed column at the final load step, coloured by displacement.

6. Colour by vertical stress. Change Coloring to stress → ZZ and rescale. The compressive stress increases steadily from zero at the top to its largest value at the base.

Figure 8: Choosing the ZZ component of stress in the Coloring menu.

docs.title: Analysing the stress variation with height
docs.text:
csv_column holds one CSV file per load step. The first line of each file is the load fraction, time, and the second line holds the column headers; after that there is one row per GIMP. The final step, mps_1_00051.csv, starts:

time,1.0000000000000004
initial position_x,initial position_y,initial position_z,position_x,position_y,position_z,stress_xx,stress_yy,stress_zz,stress_xy,stress_yz,stress_xz
0.0125,0.0125,0.0125,0.0125,0.0125,0.00634021565216069,0.0,0.0,-378.742813055138,0.0,0.0,0.0
0.0125,0.0125,0.037500000000000006,0.0125,0.0125,0.019020646956482066,0.0,0.0,-378.742813055138,0.0,0.0,0.0
0.0125,0.0125,0.0625,0.0125,0.0125,0.031765464864891575,6.107727604173849e-14,6.107727604173849e-14,-365.68430455127134,0.0,0.0,0.0
--- many more rows of data ---

initial position_z is \(z_p\) in the analytical solution, position_z is the GIMP's current height, and stress_zz is the vertical Cauchy stress in Pa.

Floating-point spellings in the raw CSV

Values such as 1.0000000000000004 and 0.037500000000000006 are the exact binary representations Julia stores for 1.0 and 0.0375, and the trailing digits of the stresses are floating-point noise.

The short Julia script below plots the stresses from the final step against the analytical solution from the Problem summary. You can run it in the same Julia session straight after the analysis, either by copying it into the REPL or by saving it as plot_stress.jl in the MPM3S folder and running include("plot_stress.jl"). It needs Plots; DelimitedFiles comes with Julia.

To install Plots, once, start Julia and, before activating MPM3S (so that Plots is not added to MPM3S itself), use:

using Pkg
Pkg.add("Plots")
The commands to run the plot are: 
using DelimitedFiles, Plots

# the final output step of the column; skip the "time" line, then read the header
data, header = readdlm("csv_column/mps_1_00051.csv", ',', Float64; skipstart=1, header=true)
column(name) = data[:, findfirst(==(name), vec(header))]
z0  = column("initial position_z")
szz = column("stress_zz")

# analytical vertical stress
ρ, g, L = 50.0, 9.81, 0.8
σ(z) = -ρ * g * (L - z)
z = range(0.0, L, length=100)

scatter(-szz, z0, label="MPM3S", xlabel="vertical compressive stress (Pa)", ylabel="initial height (m)")
plot!(-σ.(z), z, label="analytical")

Figure 10: Vertical compressive stress at the GIMPs after the final load step, plotted against their initial height, compared with the analytical solution.

The numerical stresses agree with the analytical solution to within 2% of the stress at the base (\(392.4\) Pa), with the largest differences in the elements at the base and at the free surface.

To see how the accuracy depends on the mesh, halve "element size" in Material points to 0.025 and run the problem again.

docs.title: Tutorial 2: Compaction via a rigid body
Introduction
docs.text:
This quick start tutorial introduces the concept of a rigid body interacting with the material points. It builds on Tutorial 1 and introduces the concept of a rigid body interacting with the material points.

This tutorial analyses a cube of soil compressed by a rigid cube by 25% of its height. It is used to validate that the contact formulation produces the expected uniform vertical stress and displacement fields. This problem has been used to validate our contact formulation 1 and our adaptive-octree extension 2.

This tutorial has three main sections after the introduction:

  • Input setup
  • Deploying and running the problem
  • Viewing the results

docs.title: Background: rigid-body contact
docs.text:
This tutorial extends Tutorial 1 to include normal contact. A brief overview is provided here for context; see equilibrium with rigid-body contact for the full technical details. provides a schematic overview of how the contact between the rigid body and the material points works.

When contact is detected between a GIMP and the rigid body, (a) initial state, a normal contact force is applied at the corners of the GIMP's domain to resist the overlap. This force is proportional to the amount of overlap and can be thought of as a spring whose stiffness resists the overlap. MPM3S calculates the spring stiffness automatically from the GIMP size and material properties,

\[ \epsilon_N = 50\, E_p\, A_p^0, \]

where \(E_p\) is the smallest Young's modulus of the GIMPs in the element and \(A_p^0 = (V_p^0)^{2/3}\) is a representation of the contact area, with \(V_p^0\) the initial GIMP volume. A tangential stiffness of \(25\, E_p\, A_p^0\) is used for friction. The springs are stiff but not rigid, so a small overlap between the rigid body and the GIMPs remains - a few millimetres in this problem.

After the springs have been activated the GIMPs and the mesh deform due to the contact forces created by the springs, (b) deformed state, and once convergence is obtained the mesh is reset, (c) mesh reset.

Figure 1: Schematic of the steps for penalty contact between a rigid body and a deformable GIMP domain.

docs.title: Problem summary
docs.text:
The aim is to introduce the set-up and modelling of soil-structure interaction problems. The problem is a deformable cube compressed by a rigid cube. Although simple, it is essential, as it validates the contact formulation by confirming that the overlap between the two bodies stays small and that the resulting vertical stress field is uniform throughout the cube and matches the analytical Hencky solution for the Cauchy stress in the vertical direction

\[ \sigma_{zz} = E \ln\!\left(\frac{L}{L_0}\right) \frac{L_0}{L} = \frac{10^6}{0.75} \ln(0.75) \approx -3.84 \times 10^5 \text{ Pa}, \]

where \(L_0 = 0.8\) m is the initial cube height, \(\Delta z = -0.2\) m is the prescribed compression and \(L = L_0 + \Delta z = 0.6\) m is the final height after the \(25\%\) axial compression.

As in Tutorial 1 the material is homogeneous Hencky elastic, here with \(E = 10^6\) Pa, \(\nu = 0\) and \(\rho = 1000\) kg/m\(^3\). The whole \(1.6\) m background domain is discretised by a uniform \(0.4\) m mesh (\(4 \times 4 \times 4 = 64\) elements); the soil fills \(2 \times 2 \times 2 = 8\) of them, with a \(2 \times 2 \times 2\) grid of GIMPs per element. Roller boundaries are imposed on the four side faces and the base, and the top face is left free for the rigid cube to push on.

The rigid cube is a \(1.2 \times 1.2 \times 1.0\) m box, centred over the soil, that overhangs its top by \(0.2\) m on every side. It starts resting on the soil and is pushed down \(0.2\) m over 20 load steps.

Gravity is switched off, so all of the load on the soil comes from the rigid cube.

Figure 2: The cube of soil. (a) The background mesh, with element size \(h = 0.4\) m, and (b) the \(2 \times 2 \times 2\) grid of GIMP domains in each element.

Figure 3: A vertical section through the soil and the rigid cube. Rollers act on the base and the four sides (the front and back faces are not shown), and the two rows of empty elements above the soil lie inside the rigid cube. The red dashed line marks the base of the rigid cube after the 0.2 m of compression imposed over 20 load steps.

The simulation is configured through a single JSON object - a human-readable, editable text file. It extends Tutorial 1 with a rigid body. The complete file for this problem, and the rigid cube geometry, can be found here, and every key is described on the input_data.json file format page.

docs.title: Machine and domain
docs.text:
"GPU": "off" runs the analysis on the CPU.

"domain update": "stretch" lets the GIMP domains to compress as the cube is compressed. Without it, the domains keep their initial size, and the GIMPs next to the base cannot move closer to it.

The background mesh is sized automatically to hold the soil and the same height of empty space above it, so it is a cube of side \(1.6\) m. "gravity" is zero, so the soil carries no weight.

docs.title: Material points
docs.text: The soil is one \(0.8\) m layer on a \(0.8 \times 0.8\) m footprint, discretised by \(0.4\) m elements with \(2 \times 2 \times 2\) GIMPs in each, using the elastic properties from the Problem summary.

docs.title: Rigid body
docs.text:
A rigid body is a system of one or more points. Each point has six degrees of freedom - three displacements and three rotations - and carries a mass and rotational inertia. The rigid cube is a single point at its centre, \((0.4, 0.4, 1.3)\) m.

Its "boundary conditions" list the six degrees of freedom in the order \([u_x, u_y, u_z, \theta_x, \theta_y, \theta_z]\). Five are "fixed", and the vertical displacement is prescribed as \(-0.01\) m per load step, so the rigid cube moves \(0.2\) m down over the 20 load steps. Because every degree of freedom is held, the mass and inertia have no effect.

The geometry comes from cube.stl, which sits in the same folder as the input file: the "stl" path is relative to the input file, so only file name means the same folder. It is attached to point 1 and drawn in global coordinates (the same global coordinates as point 1) with its base on the top of the soil. On the first run MPM3S builds a tetrahedral mesh of the rigid cube and saves it in cube_mesh.txt, which later runs read instead. If you change cube.stl, delete cube_mesh.txt so that the mesh is rebuilt.

docs.title: Contact
docs.text: The contact between the rigid cube and the soil is frictionless. The contact stiffness is set automatically, as described in the Background.

docs.title: Analysis
docs.text:
A single static stage of 20 load steps with the rigid body switched on. Gravity is zero, so "load": "full" has nothing to apply; all of the load comes from the rigid cube, which is pushed down a little further at every step.

"rigid body surface placement": "on" moves the rigid cube vertically at the start of the stage so that its base rests exactly on the top of the soil. Rollers are applied on the four sides and the base, and the top is free.

"adaptivity": { "type": "uniform" } meshes the whole background domain at the \(0.4\) m element size. Without it, only the elements holding material points are \(0.4\) m and the empty space is filled with coarser elements.

docs.title: Solver
docs.text: The same settings as Tutorial 1: Newton-Raphson iterations to a tolerance of \(10^{-6}\), as there are no small ovelaps in this example there is no need for ghost stabilisation.

docs.title: Output
docs.text: VTK and CSV output at every load step. The CSV files record each GIMP's position, domain size ("lp") and stress, and the rigid cube's position and reaction force - the force needed to push it - which are used in Analysing the stress in the domain.

docs.text:
MPM3S is written in the Julia programming language, and there are two ways to run the code, both explored on the deployment page. As this is a small problem that runs quickly, this tutorial uses Julia directly; see the installation guide for installing Julia and MPM3S.

Working in the MPM3S folder

The input file is read from validation_data_and_jsons/input_data_compress.json, and the output folders vtk_cube and csv_cube are written to, and read back from, the MPM3S folder.

docs.text:
The input file for this tutorial comes with MPM3S, as validation_data_and_jsons/input_data_compress.json, together with the geometry of the rigid cube, cube.stl, and its mesh cache, cube_mesh.txt; they are the same files as the ones provided here. docs.title: Running the problem
docs.text:
Julia is now running in the MPM3S folder and MPM3S loaded. The JSON file for this problem is loaded with MPM3S and is stored in the folder validation_data_and_jsons, the simulations are started with:

docs.title: Reading the output
docs.text:
Before the first load step, MPM3S reports the rigid body surface placement: the lowest point of the rigid cube (body base) and the top of the soil (material top) are both at \(0.8\) m, so the rigid cube is moved by just Δz = 2.23517e-8 m, a small tolerance above the soil.

The progress line then works as in Tutorial 1. The load fraction t rises by Δt 0.05 per load step, each step converges in 4 Newton-Raphson iterations (NR), and no steps are cut or material points deleted. The uniform background mesh has N 125 nodes, a \(5 \times 5 \times 5\) grid.

5. Choose a field to colour the GIMPs by. Select mps_1_..vtu and open the Coloring menu, which lists the fields written to the VTK files: displacement, strain and stress. docs.title: Analysing the stress in the domain
docs.text:
csv_cube/rigid_body.csv has one row per load step for the rigid cube's point, body1. The time column is the load fraction, body1_position_z is the height of the rigid cube's centre and body1_reaction force_z is the vertical force needed to push the rigid cube down, in N:

time,body1_position_x,body1_position_y,body1_position_z,body1_reaction force_x,body1_reaction force_y,body1_reaction force_z
0.05,0.4,0.4,1.290000022351742,0.0,0.0,8022.186499840163
0.1,0.4,0.4,1.280000022351742,0.0,0.0,16343.582579162323
...
1.0000000000000002,0.4,0.4,1.1000000223517419,0.0,0.0,237097.96125687487

The GIMP files, csv_cube/mps_1_00002.csv to mps_1_00021.csv, have the same layout as in Tutorial 1, with the addition of the domain half-widths lp_x, lp_y and lp_z.

The short Julia script below compares the final state with the analytical solution from the Problem summary. As in Tutorial 1, you can run it in the same Julia session straight after the analysis, either by copying it into the REPL or by saving it as check_stress.jl in the MPM3S folder and running include("check_stress.jl"). It needs only DelimitedFiles, which comes with Julia.

using DelimitedFiles

# the soil at the final load step; skip the "time" line, then read the header
soil, soil_header = readdlm("csv_cube/mps_1_00021.csv", ',', Float64; skipstart=1, header=true)
soil_column(name) = soil[:, findfirst(==(name), vec(soil_header))]
z    = soil_column("position_z")
lp_z = soil_column("lp_z")
szz  = soil_column("stress_zz")

# the rigid cube: one row per load step, so the last row is the final step
rigid, rigid_header = readdlm("csv_cube/rigid_body.csv", ',', Float64; header=true)
rigid_column(name) = rigid[end, findfirst(==(name), vec(rigid_header))]
force_z = rigid_column("body1_reaction force_z")
base_z  = rigid_column("body1_position_z") - 0.5    # the rigid cube is 1 m tall

E, L0, area = 1.0e6, 0.8, 0.8 * 0.8
L = maximum(z + lp_z)                                # final height of the soil
println("final soil height       ", round(L, digits=4), " m (overlap ", round(1000 * (L - base_z), digits=1), " mm)")
println("mean vertical stress    ", round(sum(szz) / length(szz) / 1000, digits=1), " kPa")
println("Hencky at that height   ", round(E * log(L / L0) * L0 / L / 1000, digits=1), " kPa")
println("rigid cube force / area ", round(-force_z / area / 1000, digits=1), " kPa")

For this run it prints:

final soil height       0.6046 m (overlap 4.6 mm)
mean vertical stress    -370.5 kPa
Hencky at that height   -370.5 kPa
rigid cube force / area -370.5 kPa

The rigid cube overlaps the soil by \(4.6\) mm - about \(0.6\%\) of the soil's height - so the soil is compressed to \(0.6046\) m rather than \(0.6\) m. At that height the Hencky solution gives \(-370.5\) kPa, matching the mean stress in the GIMPs; the full \(0.2\) m of compression would give the \(-383.6\) kPa of the Problem summary, \(3.5\%\) more.

The stress is uniform: every GIMP has the same vertical stress, \(-370.5\) kPa, and the rigid cube force divided by the area of the soil gives the same value.

To see the effect of the mesh, set "element size" in Material points to 0.2 and compare the overlap and the stresses.

  1. Robert E. Bird, Giuliano Pretti, William M. Coombs, Charles E. Augarde, Yaseen U. Sharif, Michael J. Brown, Gareth Carter, Catriona Macdonald, and Kirstin Johnson. A dynamic implicit 3D material point-to-rigid body contact approach for large deformation analysis. International Journal for Numerical Methods in Engineering, 2025. ↩

  2. Robert E. Bird, William M. Coombs, Charles E. Augarde, Giuliano Pretti, and Ted J. O'Hare. An implicit octree-based adaptive material point method. 2026. URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.09275, arXiv:2606.09275. ↩

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
This tutorial walks through a Cone Penetration Test (CPT) simulation, a workhorse problem in offshore geotechnical engineering that is used to calibrate soil parameters against in-situ measurements. This tuto

A rigid cone is pushed quasi-statically \(4.5\) m into a bed of dry sand, and the cone-tip resistance can be compared against centrifuge data such as that of Davidson et al. 1 and Cerfontaine et al. 2. The problem builds on Tutorial 2 and adds four things: an elasto-plastic sand whose stiffness increases with depth, frictional contact, mesh refinement that follows the cone, and an analysis made of two stages.

This tutorial has four sections:

  • Problem description
  • Input setup
  • Deploying and running the problem
  • Viewing the results

docs.title: Problem description
docs.text:
You will define the soil, the cone, the two loading stages, the solver and the output in the input file. All the inputs to the simulation are defined using the input_data.json file format.

To reduce the computational cost the symmetry of the problem is exploited and therefore only a quarter of the problem is modelled, using the two vertical planes of symmetry through the cone axis. The cone axis runs down the corner of the soil block at \(x = y = 0\), and the two faces that meet there carry roller conditions.

Figure 1: The quarter model: a \(10 \times 10 \times 20\) m block of sand with the cone above the corner at \(x = y = 0\), where the two symmetry planes meet. Rollers act on the four vertical faces and the base is fixed. The cone, \(0.8\) m across with a \(60^\circ\) tip, is not drawn to scale.

Figure adapted from 3.

Soil block: \(10 \times 10\) m in plan and \(20\) m deep, starting with \(2 \times 2 \times 2\) material points in each element. The base element size is given as \(2.0\) m, but every element size must be a power-of-two multiple of the smallest one - \(0.025\) m at the cone - so the base size becomes \(0.025 \times 2^6 = 1.6\) m and the footprint is rounded up to seven elements, \(11.2 \times 11.2\) m (see how element sizes set the mesh).

Boundary conditions: Rollers on the four vertical faces and a fixed base, at \(x = 0\) and \(y = 0\) these are the symmetry conditions. The soil surface is free.

Material: an elasto-plastic sand. Yield is governed by a frictional cone with a Willam-Warnke deviatoric section, and plastic flow by a Drucker-Prager cone set by the dilation angle, so the flow is non-associated. The elastic behaviour is linear in logarithmic (Hencky) strain. The model is described in isotropic elasto-plasticity. The sand has a relative density of \(D_r = 38\%\), and its parameters come from the Brinkgreve correlations 4:

Property Correlation Value at \(D_r = 38\%\) Input key Reference Young's modulus \(E^{ref} = 60\,000\; D_r/100\) kPa \(22.8\) MPa "E": 2.28e7 Friction angle \(\phi = 28 + 12.5\; D_r/100\) \(32.75^\circ\) "friction angle": 32.75 Dilation angle \(\psi = -2 + 12.5\; D_r/100\) \(2.75^\circ\) "dilation angle": 2.75 Dry unit weight \(\gamma = 15 + 4\; D_r/100\) kN/m\(^3\) \(16.52\) kN/m\(^3\) - Density \(\gamma = (15 + 4\; D_r/100)/10\) kg/m\(^3\) \(1.652\) kg/m\(^3\) "density": 1652.0 Stiffness exponent \(m = 0.7 - D_r/320\) \(0.58125\) "exponent": 0.58125 Earth pressure at rest \(K_0 = 1 - \sin\phi\) \(0.459\) "reference stress" (below) Poisson's ratio - \(0.25\) "nu": 0.25 Cohesion - \(0.3\) kPa "cohesion": 300.0

The density is entered as the unit weight divided by \(10\) m/s\(^2\).

The Young's modulus increases with depth. Brinkgreve's stiffness law is written in terms of the horizontal stress \(K_0 \sigma_v\) and a reference pressure \(p^{ref} = 100\) kPa, whereas MPM3S's stress-dependent stiffness uses the vertical stress \(\sigma_v\). The two are the same when the reference stress is \(p^{ref}/K_0\):

\[ E = E^{ref} \left( \frac{K_0\, \sigma_v}{p^{ref}} \right)^{m} = E^{ref} \left( \frac{\sigma_v}{\sigma^{ref}} \right)^{m}, \qquad \sigma^{ref} = \frac{p^{ref}}{K_0} = 217.85 \text{ kPa}. \]

\(\sigma_v\) is calculated from the weight of the soil above each material point's initial position, so each point's stiffness is set once and does not change during the analysis.

Cone: CPT.stl, a cylinder of radius \(r = 0.4\) m with a \(60^\circ\) conical tip, \(10.69\) m long in total and drawn with its tip at the origin. Coulomb friction with \(\mu = 0.33\) acts between the cone and the sand, and the contact penalty is set automatically, as described in Tutorial 2.

Loading: Two static stages:

  • Stage 1 - initial stresses: the cone is switched off and gravity is ramped up over 5 load steps.
  • Stage 2 - penetration: the cone is placed on the soil surface and pushed down \(10\) mm per load step for 450 load steps (\(4.5\) m), with the mesh refined to \(0.025\) m wherever the cone surface is.

Solver: Newton-Raphson, quasi-static, for both stages.

docs.title: Machine and domain
docs.text:
"GPU": "on" runs the analysis on an NVIDIA GPU. This is recommended here, because refining the cone surface to \(0.025\) m creates a large number of material points; set it to "off" to run on the CPU.

The background grid is sized automatically to hold the soil block and the empty space above it, which here makes it a cube of side \(51.2\) m. Gravity acts in \(-z\).

docs.title: Material points
docs.text:
A single \(20\) m layer of Willam-Warnke sand over a \(10 \times 10\) m footprint, with the properties from the Problem description. The "E overburden" block makes the Young's modulus increase with depth.

"extra capacity": 1.2 reserves 20% more storage than the initial material points need, because the refinement around the cone splits material points into smaller ones.

docs.title: Rigid body
docs.text:
The cone is one system with a single point, placed at its tip - the origin of CPT.stl. All positions in the file are global, so the point and the STL geometry are given in the same frame.

"offset" shifts the whole cone \(10\) mm in \(-x\) and \(-y\), so its axis sits just outside the corner of the soil block. All six degrees of freedom are "fixed", so the cone does not move and its mass and inertia play no part; stage 2 replaces the vertical condition to push the cone down.

CPT_mesh.txt stores the tetrahedral mesh of the cone. If it is missing, it is generated from the STL on the first run.

docs.title: Contact
docs.text: Coulomb friction with \(\mu = 0.33\) between the cone and the sand.

docs.title: Stage 1: initial stresses
docs.text:
The first entry in "analysis" is a static stage with the cone switched off ("rigid bodies": "off"). Gravity is ramped from zero to its full value over 5 load steps, setting up the initial stresses in the sand. "adaptivity": {"type": "none"} uses the base mesh: elements of the \(1.6\) m base size wherever there are material points, and coarser elements in the empty space above the soil.

The four vertical faces are rollers and the base is fixed. The top face is fixed too, but it lies at twice the soil depth, in the empty space above the soil, so the soil surface stays free.

docs.title: Stage 2: cone penetration
docs.text:
The second stage switches the cone on. "rigid body surface placement": "on" moves it vertically at the start of the stage so that its tip rests on the soil surface, and "load": "full" keeps gravity at its full value throughout.

"rigid body boundary conditions" replaces the conditions of point 1 of system 1 - the cone - for this stage only, prescribing a vertical displacement of \(-0.01\) m per load step. Over the 450 load steps the cone penetrates \(4.5\) m.

"rigid body surface" adaptivity refines the elements the cone surface passes through to \(0.025\) m at every step, so the fine mesh travels down with the cone. For a quicker, coarser first run use "element size": 0.1.

docs.title: Solver
docs.text:
Each load step is solved by Newton-Raphson iterations to a tolerance of \(10^{-6}\); a step that has not converged after 20 iterations is retried with half the increment.

"ghost factor" and "ghost factor mass" set the strength of the ghost stabilisation of poorly filled elements at the edges of the soil, and "poor factor": 0.25 treats elements less than a quarter full as poorly filled.

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
VTK files for ParaView are written to vtk_CPT_dr38 every \(0.5\%\) of each stage's load steps, which for the 450 load steps of stage 2 corresponds to every 2 load steps. The CSV files go to csv_CPT_dr38 every \(0.25\%\), which is every load step here.

The rigid-body CSV output includes the reaction force on the cone - the total force needed to push it, made up of the resistance at the tip and the friction along the sleeve. Cone resistance shows how the tip resistance is calculated from it.

docs.title: Deploying and running the problem
docs.text:
MPM3S is written in the Julia programming language. See the installation guide for installing Julia and MPM3S, and Tutorial 1 for a first, small run.

Working in the MPM3S folder

Julia runs in the MPM3S folder - the folder you downloaded - throughout this tutorial, and every path in the commands and scripts is relative to it. The input file is read from validation_data_and_jsons/input_data_CPT_dr38.json, and the output folders vtk_CPT_dr38 and csv_CPT_dr38 are written to, and read back from, the MPM3S folder. The CSV files exported from ParaView are saved in vtk_CPT_dr38 too.

Deployment instructions terminal 
$ julia -t auto

julia> cd("path/to/MPM3S")
julia> using Pkg; Pkg.activate(".")
  Activating project at `path/to/MPM3S`

julia> using MPM3S

julia> MPM3S.non_linear_solve("validation_data_and_jsons/input_data_CPT_dr38.json");
stage 1/2 ████████████ 100.0% t 1.0/1.0 step 6 Δt 0.2 NR 3 cuts 0 del 0 N 1640
[ Info: rigid body surface placement: body base 0.0 → material top 19.8694   Δz = 19.8694
stage 2/2 ████████████ 100.0% t 1.001/1.0 step 460 Δt 0.00222 NR 9 cuts 7 del 2133 N 57067

docs.title: Setting up the problem
docs.text:
The input file for this tutorial comes with MPM3S, as validation_data_and_jsons/input_data_CPT_dr38.json, together with the cone geometry, CPT.stl, and its mesh cache, CPT_mesh.txt; the input file is the same as the complete input file. The STL and mesh-cache paths in the input file are relative to the input file, so the files must stay in the same folder.

As in Tutorial 1, open a terminal, start Julia with every CPU thread available (-t auto), then move into the folder where you downloaded MPM3S, activate it and load MPM3S. The output folders vtk_CPT_dr38 and csv_CPT_dr38 are created in the MPM3S folder.

docs.title: Running the problem
docs.text:
Julia is now running in the MPM3S folder and MPM3S loaded. The JSON file for this problem is loaded with MPM3S and is stored in the folder validation_data_and_jsons, the simulations are started with:

MPM3S.non_linear_solve("validation_data_and_jsons/input_data_CPT_dr38.json");

This is a large analysis: with \(0.025\) m elements around the cone it is intended for a GPU or an HPC node. On a workstation without a GPU, set "GPU": "off" and use "element size": 0.1 in stage 2.

docs.title: Reading the output
docs.text:
The progress line works as in Tutorial 1, showing stage 1/2 while the initial stresses are set up and stage 2/2 during penetration.

At the start of stage 2, MPM3S reports the rigid body surface placement: the cone tip (body base, at the origin of CPT.stl) is moved up by Δz to the soil surface (material top), which has settled to \(19.87\) m under the weight of the sand.

During penetration N grows as the mesh is refined around the cone. Load steps that do not converge are retried with half the increment (cuts), and material points next to the cone that become too distorted are deleted (del).

docs.title: Viewing the results
docs.text:
Displacements and stresses

To see the displacements and stresses during the simulation, follow the same steps as for the compression cube in Tutorial 2. All the VTK files for this problem are in path/to/MPM3S/vtk_CPT_dr38. This section shows how to extract the load on the cone and its penetration from them.

docs.title: Cone resistance
docs.text:
csv_CPT_dr38/rigid_body.csv has one row per output step for the cone's point, body1. body1_position_z is the height of the cone tip and body1_reaction force_z is the vertical force needed to push the cone. Because only a quarter of the soil is modelled, the tip resistance is approximately

\[ q_c = \frac{4\, |F_z|}{\pi r^2}, \qquad r = 0.4 \text{ m}, \]

and the penetration depth is the height at which the cone is placed on the soil, minus body1_position_z. The sand settles under its own weight in stage 1, so the surface is at about \(19.87\) m rather than \(20\) m; MPM3S prints the exact value as material top in the rigid body surface placement message at the start of stage 2. \(F_z\) includes the friction along the sleeve as well as the force on the tip, which is why \(q_c\) is approximate; the published results were calculated in the same way. The rows from stage 1 come before the cone is placed on the soil, with zero force, and should be skipped. In a static stage the time column is the load fraction, which runs from 0 to 1 over the \(4.5\) m of penetration.

docs.title: Tip resistance without the sleeve friction
docs.text:
The reaction force in rigid_body.csv includes the friction along the sleeve. To find the force on the tip alone, sum the vertical contact force on the triangles of the conical tip in ParaView, and track the height of the tip:

1. Open the cone. File → Open, go to vtk_CPT_dr38, select the surface_..vtu series on its own, click OK and then Apply. The cone appears in the render view.

Figure 2: The cone surface after Apply.

2. Select the triangles of the conical tip. Click Select Cells On in the render-view toolbar (or press S) and drag a box around the conical tip, so that its triangles are highlighted in pink and the cylindrical sleeve is not. Hold Ctrl and drag again to add any triangles that were missed.

Figure 3: The triangles of the conical tip selected and highlighted in pink.

3. Find the Extract Selection filter. Open the Filters menu. Ctrl + Space opens the same filter search from anywhere in ParaView.

Figure 4: The Filters menu.

4. Extract the selection. Type extract sel, choose Extract Selection and press Enter.

Figure 5: The filter search with Extract Selection highlighted.

5. Apply it, then select the tip point. ExtractSelection1 appears in the Pipeline Browser; click Apply. It holds only the triangles of the tip. Then (1) click Clear Selection to remove the selected triangles, and (2) click Select Points On (or press D) and drag a small box around the very tip of the cone, which is highlighted as a single pink point.

Figure 6: ExtractSelection1 in the Pipeline Browser, with the tip point selected.

6. Extract the tip point and name the two extracts. Apply Extract Selection again to extract the tip point. Right-click each extract in the Pipeline Browser, choose Rename, and call the triangles cone load and the point cone tip.

Figure 7: Renaming the second extract in the Pipeline Browser.

7. Check the extracts. Hide surface_..vtu with its eye icon. Only the conical tip is left.

Figure 8: The cone load and cone tip extracts, with the full surface hidden.

8. Open a layout for the plots. Click + beside Layout #1 to open Layout #2 and choose Line Chart View.

Figure 9: A new layout with the list of views.

9. Plot the load on the tip over time. Select cone load, go to Filters, then Search, and then type plot da and choose Plot Data Over Time.

Figure 10: The filter search with Plot Data Over Time highlighted.

10. Use the cell data. The contact force is stored on the triangles, so set Field Association to Cells. Keep Only Report Selection Statistics ticked and click Apply. ParaView reads every output step, which takes a moment, and draws a quartile chart.

Figure 11: Choosing Cells for the Field Association.

11. Choose the vertical force. In Series Parameters, untick every series except contact force (2) (stats), the \(z\) component. The chart shows its average over the tip triangles, with the spread between them shaded.

Figure 12: The average vertical contact force on the tip triangles, with the quartiles shaded.

12. Show the total. Further down, untick Show Quartiles and Show Average and tick Show Sum. sum contact force (2) (stats) is the vertical force on the tip of the quarter cone, which grows steadily as the cone penetrates.

Figure 13: The summed vertical contact force on the tip against output step.

13. Export the load. File → Export View, choose Comma or Tab Delimited Files and save the chart in vtk_CPT_dr38 as load_data.csv.

Figure 14: The Export View dialog, saving load_data.csv.

14. Plot the tip height. Select cone tip and apply Plot Data Over Time again, keeping Field Association as Points, and show only Z (stats). The tip height is \(0\) in stage 1, jumps to the soil surface at about \(19.87\) m when the cone is placed at the start of stage 2, and then falls steadily as the cone is pushed down. Export it in the same way, as position_data.csv in vtk_CPT_dr38.

Figure 15: The height of the cone tip against output step.

With \(F_{tip}\) the summed vertical contact force from load_data.csv, the tip resistance of the full cone is

\[ q_c = \frac{4\, F_{tip}}{\pi r^2}, \]

and the penetration depth is the height at which the cone is placed on the soil - \(19.8694\) m, the material top in the rigid body surface placement message - minus the tip height from position_data.csv. Both files have one row per output step; the first rows, from stage 1, have a tip height of \(0\) and are skipped.

The short Julia script below plots \(q_c\) against the penetration depth. Run it from the MPM3S folder, either by copying it into the REPL or by saving it as plot_qc.jl and running include("plot_qc.jl"). It needs Plots, installed as described in Tutorial 1.

using DelimitedFiles, Plots

# the two files exported from ParaView, one row per output step
load, _ = readdlm("vtk_CPT_dr38/load_data.csv", ',', Float64; header=true)
tip,  _ = readdlm("vtk_CPT_dr38/position_data.csv", ',', Float64; header=true)
F = load[:, 2]    # vertical contact force on the tip of the quarter cone (N)
z = tip[:, 2]     # height of the cone tip (m)

# skip stage 1, before the cone is placed on the soil (tip height 0)
s2 = z .> 0

r = 0.4               # cone radius (m)
z_surface = 19.8694   # "material top" in the rigid body surface placement message
depth = (z_surface .- z[s2])/r
qc = 4 .* F[s2] ./ (π * r^2) ./ 1e6   # tip resistance of the full cone (MPa)

plot(qc, depth, yflip=true, label="MPM3S", xlabel="tip resistance q_c (MPa)", ylabel="normalised penetration depth (m/m)")

Figure 16: Tip resistance against penetration depth normalised by the cone radius, from the script above.

Physical modelling to demonstrate the feasibility of screw piles for offshore jacket supported wind energy structures. Géotechnique, 72(2):108–126, 2022. ↩

  2. B. Cerfontaine, J. Knappett, M.J. Brown, C. Davidson, and Y. Sharif. Optimised design of screw anchors in tension in sand for renewable energy applications. Ocean Engineering, 217:108010, 2020. ↩

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
This tutorial walks through a 3D simulation of a seabed cable plough being dragged horizontally through dry sand, the most geometrically complex problem in the MPM3S tutorial set.

The plough is held at a fixed embedment depth and pulled at constant speed; the steady-state horizontal pull (tow) force is compared against the 50g geotechnical centrifuge measurements of Robinson et al. 1, with scaling to the 1g full-scale problem following Robinson et al. 2. The problem exercises contact with a non-convex rigid body, large deformation around a moving wedge, and adaptive mesh refinement that follows the plough through the domain.

This tutorial has four sections:

  • Problem description
  • Input setup
  • Deploying and running the problem
  • Viewing the results

docs.title: Problem description
docs.text:
You will define the geometry, mesh, boundary conditions, material, rigid body and solver in the input file. All the inputs to the simulation are defined using the input_data.json file format.

Only half of the domain is modelled, exploiting the symmetry of the plough in \(x\). The plough is held at a fixed embedment depth of \(D = 1.85\) m and is dragged through the soil over a total horizontal travel of \(20\) m at a step size of \(0.025\) m.

Figure 1: Initial numerical setup of the half-symmetric plough domain, showing the plough geometry, the soil block dimensions, and the Signorini exit face (C).

Figure 2: Side view of Signorini boundary conditions.

Figure 3: Schematic of the plough

Mesh: Half-symmetric domain dimensions \(L_x = 20\) m, \(L_y = 10\) m, \(L_z = 7.5\) m. As in Tutorial 3, adaptive octree refinement is driven by the rigid body position. The smallest element size near the plough surface is \(dx_{\min}\), and the surrounding "buffer" region uses elements of size \(2\, dx_{\min}\). For a quick first run set \(dx_{\min} = 0.2\) m; for a high-accuracy comparison against the experimental data drop to \(dx_{\min} = 0.075\) m. Try the values \(dx_{\min} \in \{0.075,\, 0.15,\, 0.2\}\) m to reproduce the validation envelope reported in 1.

Initial GIMP distribution: \(2\times2\times2\) material points within each element, filling the soil domain.

Boundary conditions: Roller boundaries on the symmetry plane and the remaining lateral faces, and on the base. The top face is left as a free surface (homogeneous Neumann). The face the plough exits through (marked C in ) carries a Signorini condition - material can move away from this face but not across it. Pragmatically, this is enforced by a secondary frictionless rigid plate.

Material: Hencky hyperelastic-perfectly plastic dry sand with a non-associated Drucker-Prager flow potential, calibrated to the Robinson 2019 centrifuge sand via the Brinkgreve correlations 3. Use the same parameters as Tutorial 3 and adjust the relative density to match your target. Per 1, the simulation runs at full scale with \(1g\) gravity (the \(50g\) centrifuge scaling collapses to identical \(1g\) behaviour when length and time are scaled equally 2).

Rigid body: The plough geometry includes a forward wedge, a main share and an angled mouldboard (see ). The side view of the Signorini boundary condition arrangement is shown in . To prevent rigid-body penetration of GIMPs, all convex edges sharper than \(90^\circ\) are filleted to a radius equal to half the minimum GIMP side length (~10 fillet segments per \(90^\circ\)). Frictional contact uses the same penalty parameters as Tutorial 2: \(\epsilon_N = 50\,E_p A_p\) and \(\epsilon_T = 25\,E_p A_p\).

Loading: A two-stage pseudo-static solution:

  • Stage 1 - gravity and initial embedment: Apply gravity and position the plough at its operating depth \(D = 1.85\) m.
  • Stage 2 - horizontal drag: Pull the plough horizontally in \(+y\) at a fixed depth over \(20\) m total travel, in steps of \(0.025\) m. If a step fails to converge, halve the step size and restart that step.

Solver: Newton-Raphson, quasi-static. The plough is the most complex contact geometry in the tutorial set, so robust step-size control is important.

docs.title: Mesh data
docs.text:
The half-symmetric domain, with octree refinement driven by the rigid body.

dx refined is the smallest element size, used on elements intersecting the plough surface. buffer multiplier sets the element size in the surrounding region as a multiple of dx refined.

Refinement type is rigid body adaptive so the mesh re-refines as the plough advances through the soil, matching the scheme used in Tutorial 3.

docs.title: Initial GIMP distribution
docs.text: The default \(2\times2\times2\) distribution per element, filling the soil domain.

docs.title: Boundary conditions
docs.text: Rollers everywhere except the top face (default free surface) and the exit face which uses Signorini contact.

docs.title: Material
docs.text: A single layer of hyperelastic-perfectly plastic sand, calibrated to the Robinson 2019 sand via the Brinkgreve correlations - use the same property block as Tutorial 3, adjusting the relative density to match the experimental sand.

docs.title: Rigid body
docs.text: The plough geometry is loaded from an external mesh file. Convex edges sharper than \(90^\circ\) are filleted to a radius equal to half the minimum GIMP side length.

docs.title: Loading
docs.text: The two stages: gravity plus initial embedment, then horizontal drag. The drag step size is reduced by half on a failed convergence.

docs.title: Solver
docs.text: Newton-Raphson, quasi-static. The same solver is applied to both stages.

docs.title: Output data
docs.text: VTU and VTK output is enabled for visualisation in ParaView (or VisIt). The text data field tags the run as plough for post-processing.

docs.title: Viewing the results
docs.text:
The deformed soil state at \(10\) m plough travel, with the GIMPs coloured by \(x\)-displacement (red 3 m, blue 0 m), shows how material flows around the wedge and is pushed forward (see ):

Figure 4: Deformed GIMP positions coloured according to x-displacement (red 3 m, blue 0 m) for a plough embedded 10 m into the soil at dx = 0.075 m.

Figure reproduced from 4.

After post-processing each run, plot the horizontal pull force as a function of plough position and overlay the centrifuge data of 1 for the three mesh refinements - see :

Figure 5: Comparison of numerical pull force vs plough position against centrifuge data, for the three mesh refinements dx = 0.075, 0.15, 0.2 m.

Figure reproduced from 4.

The first \(7.45\) m of travel is the embedment phase, during which the force oscillates as different parts of the plough engage with the soil. Beyond that the force reaches a steady-state regime - this is the regime to compare against the experimental measurement. Refinement consistently moves the numerical result towards the experimental data; \(dx \in \{0.075,\, 0.15\}\) m give good agreement with no parameter tuning.

  1. S. Robinson, M.J. Brown, H. Matsui, A. Brennan, C.E. Augarde, W.M. Coombs, and M. Cortis. A cone penetration test (CPT) approach to cable plough performance prediction based upon centrifuge model testing. Canadian Geotechnical Journal, 58(10):1466–1477, 2021. ↩↩↩↩

  2. Scott Robinson, Michael John Brown, Hidetake Matsui, Andrew Brennan, Charles Augarde, Will Coombs, and Michael Cortis. Centrifuge testing to verify scaling of offshore pipeline ploughs. International Journal of Physical Modelling in Geotechnics, 19(6):305–317, 2019. ↩↩

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
This is the first dynamic tutorial in MPM3S. A rigid sphere rolls down a slope under gravity, and the distance it travels is compared against the analytical slip/stick solution for a range of friction coefficients.

The problem validates frictional contact and dynamic time integration together. As the sphere moves, the elements beneath it are refined to a fine mesh that travels with it, and a boundary track keeps only the part of the slope around the sphere active.

This tutorial has four sections:

  • Problem description
  • Input setup
  • Deploying and running the problem
  • Viewing the results

docs.title: Problem description
docs.text:
You will define the slope, the sphere, the dynamic stage, the solver and the output in the input file. All the inputs to the simulation are defined using the input_data.json file format.

To keep the slope aligned with the background grid, the slope is kept horizontal and gravity is tilted by \(45^\circ\) instead (see ). The sphere then rolls along \(+x\) under the in-plane component of gravity.

Figure 1: The rolling sphere problem: a \(12.8 \times 1.6 \times 0.8\) m slab of \(0.8\) m elements with a \(2 \times 2 \times 2\) grid of GIMPs in each. The elements beneath the sphere are refined, shown schematically as one level (the finest elements are \(0.025\) m), and their GIMPs follow the refined mesh. The sphere, of radius \(1\) m, rests on the slab, and gravity is tilted \(45^\circ\) towards \(+x\). The ends and base of the slab are fixed and its sides are rollers.

Figure adapted from 1.

Slope: A slab \(12.8\) m long, \(1.6\) m wide and \(0.8\) m thick, made of \(0.8\) m base elements with \(2 \times 2 \times 2\) material points in each. The elements the sphere touches are refined to \(0.025\) m.

Boundary conditions: The two ends of the slab (\(x = 0\) and \(x = 12.8\) m) and its base are fixed, and its two sides are rollers. The top surface is free.

Material: A very stiff Hencky elastic slab: Young's modulus \(E = 10^9\) Pa, Poisson's ratio \(\nu = 0\) and density \(\rho = 1000\) kg/m\(^3\). It deforms negligibly, but modelling it with material points is what exercises the contact between a rigid body and a refined mesh - the point of the test.

Sphere: sphere.stl, a sphere of radius \(r = 1\) m made of 3120 triangles on a latitude-longitude grid, drawn centred on the origin. Its point is at the centre, with mass \(m = 5000\) kg and rotational inertia \(I = \tfrac{2}{5} m r^2 = 2000\) kg\(\cdot\)m\(^2\), a solid sphere. The sphere can move in \(x\) and \(z\) and rotate about \(y\); its other three degrees of freedom are fixed.

Friction: The friction coefficient \(\mu\) is the parameter you sweep. Try \(\mu \in \{0,\, 0.1,\, 0.2,\, 0.4,\, 1.0\}\) to cover both the slipping (\(\tan\theta_s > 3.5\mu\)) and sticking regimes.

Loading: A single dynamic stage lasting \(1\) s, with a time step of \(0.005\) s. Gravity is applied as a tilted vector

\[ g_i = 9.81 \times \left[ \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}},\, 0,\, -\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \right] \text{ m/s}^2, \]

equivalent to a \(45^\circ\) slope under vertical gravity.

Solver: Newton-Raphson, implicit dynamic. The sphere's velocity, angular velocity and rotation evolve through time under gravity and contact.

The analytical solution to compare against is the distance the sphere has travelled along \(+x\) as a function of time:

\[ d_x(t) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{g t^2}{2} \left[ \sin\theta_s - \mu \cos\theta_s \right] & \text{slipping, } \tan\theta_s > 3.5\mu \\[6pt] \dfrac{5\, g t^2 \sin\theta_s}{14} & \text{sticking, otherwise} \end{cases} \]

with \(g = 9.81\) m/s\(^2\) and \(\theta_s = 45^\circ\).

]

docs.title: Machine and domain
docs.text:
"GPU": "off" runs the analysis on the CPU. The background grid is sized automatically to hold the slab, and its \(12.8\) m length makes the grid a \(12.8\) m cube.

"gravity" is the tilted vector from the Problem description: its two non-zero components are \(9.81/\sqrt{2} \approx 6.93672\) m/s\(^2\).

docs.title: Material points
docs.text: A single \(0.8\) m layer over a \(12.8 \times 1.6\) m footprint, with the stiff elastic properties from the Problem description. The refinement size used later, \(0.025\) m, is \(0.8/2^5\), so the base element size needs no rounding.

docs.title: Rigid body
docs.text:
The sphere is one system with one point at its centre. The point's six boundary conditions, in the order \([u_x, u_y, u_z, \theta_x, \theta_y, \theta_z]\), leave it free to move in \(x\) and \(z\) and to rotate about \(y\).

sphere.stl is drawn centred on the origin, the same place as the point. "offset" then places the whole sphere with its centre above \(x = 1.5\) m, halfway across the slab's width and \(1.8\) m up - resting on the slab surface at \(0.8\) m.

docs.title: Contact
docs.text: The friction coefficient between the sphere and the slab, here \(\mu = 0.2\). This is below \(\tan(45^\circ)/3.5 \approx 0.286\), so the sphere slips as it rolls. Change it between runs to reproduce the friction sweep, and change the output directory names to match so the runs do not overwrite each other.

docs.title: Analysis
docs.text:
A single dynamic stage: \(1\) s of motion in steps of \(0.005\) s. The Newmark parameters \(\beta = 0.5\) and \(\gamma = 1.0\) add numerical damping, which keeps the stiff contact stable. "rigid body surface placement": "on" makes sure the sphere starts exactly on the slab surface.

"rigid body surface" adaptivity refines the elements the sphere's surface passes through to \(0.025\) m at every step. The slab's ends and base are fixed and its sides are rollers.

"boundary track" makes the \(x\) boundaries follow the sphere: a fixed plane at the back of the sphere deletes the slab it leaves behind ("remove": "yes"), and a fixed plane \(1\) m ahead of it keeps the slab further ahead inactive until the sphere approaches. Tracking is "off" in \(y\) and \(z\).

docs.title: Solver
docs.text: Newton-Raphson iterations to a tolerance of \(10^{-6}\) in each time step, with at most 20 iterations before the step is retried with half the time step. The ghost stabilisation uses "ghost factor": 10.0 for the stiffness and "ghost factor mass": 0.25 for the mass.

docs.title: Output
docs.text: "vtk percent": 0 writes a VTK frame at every time step, with every field, to vtk_sphere_mu0.2. The CSV output writes no material-point files (an empty list) but records the sphere's position, velocity, acceleration and angular velocity in csv_sphere_mu0.2/rigid_body.csv.

docs.title: Deploying and running the problem
docs.text:
MPM3S is written in the Julia programming language. See the installation guide for installing Julia and MPM3S, and Tutorial 1 for a first, small run.

Working in the MPM3S folder

Julia runs in the MPM3S folder - the folder you downloaded - throughout this tutorial, and every path in the commands and scripts is relative to it. The input file is read from validation_data_and_jsons/input_data_sphere.json, and the output folders vtk_sphere_mu0.2 and csv_sphere_mu0.2 are written to, and read back from, the MPM3S folder.

Deployment instructions terminal 
$ julia -t auto

julia> cd("path/to/MPM3S")
julia> using Pkg; Pkg.activate(".")
  Activating project at `path/to/MPM3S`

julia> using MPM3S

julia> MPM3S.non_linear_solve("validation_data_and_jsons/input_data_sphere.json");
[ Info: rigid body surface placement: body base 0.8 → material top 0.8   Δz = 1.87755e-7
stage 1/1 ████████████ 100.0% t 1.0/1.0 step 201 Δt 0.005 NR 4 cuts 0 del 0 N 109572

docs.title: Setting up the problem
docs.text:
The input file for this tutorial comes with MPM3S, as validation_data_and_jsons/input_data_sphere.json, together with the sphere geometry, sphere.stl, and its mesh cache, sphere_mesh.txt; the input file is the same as the complete input file. The STL and mesh-cache paths in the input file are relative to the input file, so the files must stay in the same folder.

As in Tutorial 1, open a terminal, start Julia with every CPU thread available (-t auto), then move into the folder where you downloaded MPM3S, activate it and load MPM3S. The output folders are created in the MPM3S folder.

docs.title: Running the problem
docs.text:
Julia is now running in the MPM3S folder and MPM3S loaded. The JSON file for this problem is loaded with MPM3S and is stored in the folder validation_data_and_jsons, the simulations are started with:

MPM3S.non_linear_solve("validation_data_and_jsons/input_data_sphere.json");

The analysis runs on a workstation CPU but takes a while; set "GPU": "on" if a GPU is available.

docs.title: Reading the output
docs.text:
Before the first time step, MPM3S reports the rigid body surface placement: the lowest point of the sphere (body base) and the top of the slab (material top) are both at \(0.8\) m, so the sphere is moved by only Δz = 1.87755e-7 m.

The progress line works as in Tutorial 1, except that in a dynamic stage t is the simulated time, out of the \(1\) s final time. The \(200\) time steps of Δt 0.005 s end at step 201, each converging in about 4 Newton-Raphson iterations (NR) with no steps cut or material points deleted. N is large, over \(100\,000\) nodes, because the mesh is refined to \(0.025\) m around the sphere.

docs.title: Viewing the results
docs.text:
Watching the sphere roll

The VTK files in path/to/MPM3S/vtk_sphere_mu0.2 can be opened in ParaView to watch the sphere roll, following the same steps as for the compression cube in Tutorial 2. Everything needed to check the result is in rigid_body.csv, used below.

docs.title: Distance travelled
docs.text:
csv_sphere_mu0.2/rigid_body.csv has one row per time step. The distance travelled is $d_x = $ body1_position_x \(- 1.5\) m, to be plotted against the time column and compared with \(d_x(t)\) from the Problem description. When the sphere sticks, it rolls without slipping, so body1_angular velocity_y equals body1_velocity_x (the radius is \(1\) m); when it slips, the angular velocity lags behind.

The short Julia script below compares the distance travelled with the analytical solution. Run it from the MPM3S folder, either by copying it into the REPL or by saving it as distance.jl and running include("distance.jl"). It needs Plots, installed as described in Tutorial 1.

using DelimitedFiles, Plots

# one row per time step for the sphere's point, body1
data, header = readdlm("csv_sphere_mu0.2/rigid_body.csv", ',', Float64; header=true)
column(name) = data[:, findfirst(==(name), vec(header))]
t  = column("time")
dx = column("body1_position_x") .- 1.5   # distance travelled (m)

# analytical solution: the sphere slips if tan θ > 3.5 μ, otherwise it rolls without slipping
g, θ, μ = 9.81, π/4, 0.2
slipping = tan(θ) > 3.5μ
a = slipping ? g * (sin(θ) - μ * cos(θ)) : 5/7 * g * sin(θ)   # acceleration along x (m/s²)
dx_exact = a .* t.^2 ./ 2

println(slipping ? "slipping" : "sticking")
println("distance after 1 s: MPM3S ", round(dx[end], digits=3), " m, analytical ", round(dx_exact[end], digits=3), " m")

plot(t, dx_exact, label="analytical", xlabel="time (s)", ylabel="distance travelled (m)")
scatter!(t[1:5:end], dx[1:5:end], label="MPM3S", markersize=3)

For this run it prints:

slipping
distance after 1 s: MPM3S 2.77 m, analytical 2.775 m

Figure 2: Distance travelled by the sphere against time for mu = 0.2, compared with the analytical slipping solution.

The second script, run after the first, compares the speed of the sphere's centre, \(v_x\), with the speed of its surface, \(r\omega\). With \(\mu = 0.2\) the sphere slips, so \(r\omega\) grows more slowly than \(v_x\); with \(\mu \geq 0.286\) it rolls without slipping and the two lines lie on top of each other.

# run after distance.jl, which reads the data and sets t, g, θ, μ, a and slipping
vx = column("body1_velocity_x")           # speed of the centre (m/s)
ω  = column("body1_angular velocity_y")   # spin (rad/s)
r  = 1.0                                   # sphere radius (m)

# analytical: the centre speeds up at a; while slipping, friction spins the sphere up at 5μg cos θ / 2r
v_exact  = a .* t
rω_exact = slipping ? 2.5 * μ * g * cos(θ) .* t : v_exact

plot(t, v_exact, label="v_x analytical", xlabel="time (s)", ylabel="speed (m/s)")
plot!(t, rω_exact, label="r ω analytical")
scatter!(t[1:5:end], vx[1:5:end], label="v_x MPM3S", markersize=3)
scatter!(t[1:5:end], r .* ω[1:5:end], label="r ω MPM3S", markersize=3)

Figure 3: Speed of the sphere's centre and of its surface against time for mu = 0.2, compared with the analytical slipping solution.

  1. Robert E. Bird, William M. Coombs, Charles E. Augarde, Giuliano Pretti, and Ted J. O'Hare. An implicit octree-based adaptive material point method. 2026. URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.09275, arXiv:2606.09275. ↩
